'''''Sherardia''''' is a [[Monotypic taxon|monotypic]] [[genus]] of [[flowering plant]]s in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Rubiaceae]]. The genus contains only one [[species]], '''''Sherardia arvensis''''', the '''(blue) field madder''', which is widespread across most of [[Europe]] and northern [[North Africa|Africa]] as well as southwest and central Asia (from [[Turkey]] to [[Saudi Arabia]] to [[Kazakhstan]]) and [[Macaronesia]] ([[Canary Islands]], [[Azores]], [[Madeira]], [[Savage Islands]]).<ref name="WCSP">{{cite web |url=https://wcsp.science.kew.org/namedetail.do?name_id=190923 |title=''Sherardia'' |publisher=World Checklist of Selected Plant Families (WCSP) |access-date=28 October 2021 |archive-date=28 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211028105543/https://wcsp.science.kew.org/namedetail.do?name_id=190923 |url-status=live }}</ref> It is also reportedly naturalized in [[Australia]], [[New Zealand]], [[Taiwan]], [[Kerguelen Islands|Kerguelen]], [[Ethiopia]], [[Sudan]], southern [[Africa]], [[Mexico]], [[Costa Rica]], [[South America]], [[Bermuda]], [[Cuba]], [[Haiti]] and much of [[Canada]] and the [[United States]] (especially the [[Pacific States]] and the lower [[Mississippi Valley]]).<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=190927 |title=Kew ==Description==
''Sherardia arvensis'' is an [[annual plant]] with trailing and upright stems growing up to {{cvt|40|cm}} long, having a square cross-section.  The rough pointed bristly leaves of about {{cvt|1|cm}} in length are in [[Whorl (botany)|whorls]] of four to six (normally six at the ends of the shoots, but four nearer the root).

The tiny pale lilac or pink flowers are approximately {{cvt|3|mm}} in diameter and have a long tube, with only the end part of the four petals free.  The flowers grow in clusters of two or three together in an [[involucral bract|involucral]] structure formed out of a ring of six [[bracts]].

The fruit are dry and about {{cvt|3|mm}} long with two lobes giving rise to two small, dry, indehiscent fruits called nutlets.

The four-angled stems with whorls of bristly leaves and tiny flowers are reminiscent of the [[Galium|Bedstraws]] and other related [[Rubiaceae]], but ''Sherardia'' is distinguished by its mauve/pink flowers that are organized in clusters and having a long corolla tube.<ref name=CTW>{{cite book|author1=Clapham AR |author2=Tutin TG |author3=Warburg EF |title=Excursion Flora of the British Isles|edition=3|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge|year=1981|page=299}}</ref><ref name=UCIPM>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ipm.ucdavis.edu/PMG/WEEDS/field_madder.html|title=Field madder on UC IPM Online|access-date=2010-09-07|archive-date=2010-08-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100823133922/http://www.ipm.ucdavis.edu/PMG/WEEDS/field_madder.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

''Sherardia arvensis'' plants are hermaphroditic and pollinated by flies.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Sherardia+arvensis |title=Plants for a Future - Sherardia arvensis |access-date=2019-04-30 |archive-date=2021-01-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210125182227/https://pfaf.org/User/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Sherardia+arvensis |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Uses==
''Sherardia arvensis'' is a common weed of fields, pasture, [[grassland]], and disturbed areas.<ref name=UCIPM/> The fleshy roots, though much inferior to the common madder (''[[Rubia tinctorum]]''), are sometimes used for the production of a red dye.<ref name="Georgia1914">{{cite book|author=Georgia AE|year=1914|title=A manual of weeds|publisher=The Macmillan Company|chapter=Sherardia arvensis|url=http://chestofbooks.com/flora-plants/weeds/Manual-Of-Weeds/Blue-Field-Madder-Sherardia-Arvensis-L-Spurwort-Herb-She.html|archive-date=2010-07-21|access-date=2010-09-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100721114357/http://chestofbooks.com/flora-plants/weeds/Manual-Of-Weeds/Blue-Field-Madder-Sherardia-Arvensis-L-Spurwort-Herb-She.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The genus and species were described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in ''[[Hortus Cliffortianus]]'' in 1736<ref name=HortCliff>{{cite book|author=Linnaeus C|title=Hortus Cliffortianus|publisher=George Clifford|location=Amsterdam|year=1737|page=33|url=http://caliban.mpiz-koeln.mpg.de/linne/hortus/high/IMG_1164.html|archive-date=2012-03-06|access-date=2010-09-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120306021041/http://caliban.mpiz-koeln.mpg.de/linne/hortus/high/IMG_1164.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and also appeared in his masterwork ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' in 1753.<ref name=SpPl>{{cite book|author=Linnaeus C|title=Species Plantarum|year=1753|volume=1|page=102|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/358121|archive-date=2021-12-26|access-date=2018-02-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211226181112/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/358121|url-status=live}}</ref> The genus was named in memory of the prominent English botanist [[William Sherard]] (1659–1728).<ref name=HortCliff/> The Latin epithet ''arvensis'' means that it is found in fields.
